newsitem.title: Nicaragua: Nicaragua president sworn in as bomb plot foiled.
newsitem.headline: Nicaragua president sworn in as bomb plot foiled.

text.p: Right-winger Arnoldo Aleman, taking the oath as Nicaragua's president on Friday, offered to open up talks with the Sandinistas to quell a growing threat of social unrest from the left.

Even as Aleman extended the olive branch to his political enemies, police said they had arrested two men who planned a dynamite attack against Aleman's Liberal Alliance headquarters, and possibly the president himself.
Police Subcommander Eduardo Cuadra told a news conference the men were arrested with dynamite and a detonator in their car outside Liberal headquarters before midnight on Thursday.
One of the men was a former police officer who now works as a legal adviser to the Sandinista-owned television station Channel 4, Cuadra said.
Although Aleman told reporters he would like to ask the Sandinistas about the foiled bombing attempt, he sounded a conciliatory note in his speech.

"I extend the fraternal, open and frank hand of friendship and invite our political competitors, particularly the FSLN (Sandinista National Liberation Front) to dialogue," a beaming Aleman said to 10,000 well-wishers and seven Latin American presidents under the scorching sun in the national stadium.
Aleman's inauguration was the first in modern Nicaraguan history that an elected, civilian government handed power to another, and his supporters celebrated with blue and white balloons.
Aleman, a 50-year-old lawyer and coffee grower who relishes his nickname "Fatman," rolled into the half-filled stadium in his open-topped red Mercedes-Benz, dubbed the "Fatmobile" by his supporters.

Amid booming cannons, National Assembly president Ivan Escobar Fornos placed a blue-and-white presidential sash over the burly shoulders of Aleman, who has promised a new era of democracy and prosperity to Nicaragua, the second-poorest country in the Americas after Haiti.

Aleman urged Nicaraguans to "forgive and forget" regarding the country's war-ravaged, authoritarian past, which took a turn when outgoing president Violeta Chamorro, 67, defeated the Sandinistas in 1990.
"We will not return to the past," Aleman said. "The long, dark night is over for Nicaragua."

Chamorro, an ailing, silver-haired former housewife who had been Latin America's only female head of state, was greeted by cheering when she entered the stadium, using a walking stick on her last day in office.

The ceremony coincided with the 19th anniversary of the assassination of her husband, newspaper publisher Pedro Joaquin Chamorro. His death helped spark the Sandinista uprising that toppled dictator Anastasio Somoza in 1979.
The Sandinistas, who led Nicaragua through revolutionary rule between 1979-1990, boycotted the ceremony, warned of street protests and there was violence in the countryside.

In a chilling reminder of past violence, an unknown armed group on Thursday ambushed an army patrol, killing six Nicaraguan soldiers -- including a major and two captains -- in the central province of Matagalpa, the army said.
